Family history

Looking for a Morrisite ancestor? Look up the name. The name index lists everyone on the 1861–62 roll and everyone else the sources name, with links to every place the guide mentions them. Try other spellings: the roll was printed from Danish, Swedish, Welsh and English names, and clerks spelled them as they heard them. The search box at the top of every page searches the whole site. Read what the guide has found. On the roll, a name may carry a note on what the sources say, a FamilySearch link, a tag for the men taken at Kington Fort in 1862, or a link to a person page with a life, family on the roll and sources. Check the family in Family Tree. FamilySearch links marked “probable” are likely but not certain; Family Tree is shared and editable, so check its sources before relying on it. See where the records are. The place pages gather what the guide holds on each place the family lived. Repositories lists the archives that hold Morrisite papers, court files and land records, and Documents lists what can be read online. Share what your family knows. Letters, photographs, family histories and corrections are welcome; see Share records. Descendants have already filled in parts of this guide.

Essential works The movement's own scripture, a later compilation from within the movement, and the only book-length history of it. Primary text · 1886 The Spirit Prevails Joseph Morris's revelations, articles, and letters, recorded from 1857 to 1862 and published after his death by his follower George S. Dove. It holds more than 300 revelations, making Morris one of the most prolific revelators in Mormon history. For his followers it was scripture. Read online: Internet Archive · Google Books. Both are free scans of the University of California copy (684 pages). Primary text · 1899 Gems of Inspiration A Collection of Sublime Thoughts by Modern Prophets, compiled by John R. Eardley, a leader of the Montana church after Williams’s death, and printed in San Francisco by Joseph A. Dove in 1899. It shows how the movement kept and passed on its prophetic writings a generation after Morris. Read online: Internet Archive. The standard history · three editions C. LeRoy Anderson's history of the Morrisites 1981 For Christ Will Come Tomorrow: The Saga of the Morrisites 1988 Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites, 2nd ed. 2010 Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites (Revisited), the final edition. Buy from the publisher · Digital edition (member libraries) Anderson, a sociologist at the University of Montana, built the book on Morrisite papers found in a Deer Lodge attic and on the records of Andrew Hendrikson, who presided over the Montana church from 1886 to 1921, kept by his family. His research files are the core of the Morrisite collection at USU. The 2010 edition is in print in paperback and as an ebook. Please buy it from Utah State University Press, an imprint of the University Press of Colorado; buying from the publisher supports keeping the book in print.

t: Mark H. Forscutt on Joseph Morris
s: Mark H. Forscutt on Joseph Morris Forscutt (1834–1903) was clerk of the Morrisite First Council and an apostle in Morris's church, and later a minister in the Reorganized Church. He wrote about the movement at least twice. “Sketch of Joseph Morris,” undated CHL MS 702 · edition in preparation Original Church History Library, Salt Lake City, MS 702. Manuscript, 54 leaves, in Forscutt’s hand. Catalog record and images Copy Morrisite collection, Utah State University, USU CAINE COLL MSS 10, box 3, folder 1 Date Written some years after Forscutt joined the RLDS Church Contents An insider’s history of the movement: the setting in Utah after Joseph Smith’s death, Morris’s call and claims, the organization of the church in April 1861, its theology and revelations, its relations with the Reorganized Church, the mounting conflict with the territorial authorities, and the opening of the siege of Kington Fort on June 13, 1862, which Forscutt witnessed. The narrative ends with the first cannon shot. Utah State University’s description says the last page refers to an earlier history Forscutt wrote; this is being checked against the original. Edition A documentary edition, with an introductory essay and annotation, is in preparation by Eric Paul Rogers. The text is not published here in the meantime; short passages are quoted and cited elsewhere in this guide. Partial history of the Morrisite church, ca. 1862 U of U MS 0261 Held by J. Willard Marriott Library Special Collections, University of Utah (photostat copy, 1 folder) Contents A contemporary account focused on events, with Forscutt's view of the LDS leadership. Possibly the earlier history the “Sketch” is said to refer to. Access Finding aid Further reading: Eric Paul Rogers, “Mark Hill Forscutt: Mormon Missionary, Morrisite Apostle, RLDS Minister,” John Whitmer Historical Association Journal 21 (2001): 69–100. t: 1857–1862Joseph Morris, an English convert to the Latter-day Saint chu…
s: 1857–1862Joseph Morris, an English convert to the Latter-day Saint church, records the revelations later gathered as The Spirit Prevails. He writes repeatedly to Brigham Young. No written reply is known; Anderson reports that the first letter, dated December 7, 1857, bears a penciled note on its margin, “He’s weak minded.” The church’s answer comes in February 1861 (next entry).

t: 11 Feb 1861The apostles John Taylor and Wilford Woodruff hold a meetin…
s: 11 Feb 1861The apostles John Taylor and Wilford Woodruff hold a meeting at South Weber to “regulate” the branch. On Taylor’s motion, seconded by Woodruff, sixteen of Morris’s followers are cut off from the church, among them Bishop Richard Cook, his brother John Cook, John Parson and Robert Farley (Woodruff’s journal, February 11, 1861). Morris’s name is not on the list Woodruff recorded. 6 Apr 1861Morris organizes the Church of the Firstborn and calls his followers to gather at Kington Fort, an abandoned 1853 settler fort at South Weber. 1861–1862The community holds its goods in common and awaits the Second Coming. As appointed days pass, some members grow discontented and try to leave.

t: 11 Jun 1862Acting Governor Frank Fuller orders General Daniel H. Wells…
s: 11 Jun 1862Acting Governor Frank Fuller orders General Daniel H. Wells to furnish the territorial marshal, Henry W. Lawrence, and his deputies, Robert T. Burton and Theodore McKean, “a sufficient military force” to act as a posse in serving Third District Court writs for the arrest of “Joseph Morris and others residing in the northern part of Davis County.” The order survives in a copy Wells made in 1871 (Utah Territorial Militia Records, series 2210, document 1,215, Utah State Archives; page image on FamilySearch). 13–15 Jun 1862A territorial posse under Robert T. Burton besieges the fort. Morris and John Banks are killed during the surrender; eleven people die in all, including two young posse members, Jared Smith (June 13) and Peter Wahler (June 15). 18–19 Jun 1862Before Judge Kinney in Salt Lake City, Richard Cook is fined and jailed for contempt, Peter Klemgaard and Christian Neilson are held in prison, and ninety-five other men are bound over on $1,500 bail each for the March 1863 term (Deseret News, June 25, 1862).

t: Mar 1863In Salt Lake City, seven Morrisites are convicted of second-de…
s: Mar 1863In Salt Lake City, seven Morrisites are convicted of second-degree murder: Peter Klemgard is sentenced to fifteen years, Christian Neilsen to twelve, and Abraham Taylor, Kadrup Neilsen, Jens Christiansen, Andrew Lee and Andrew M. Mason to ten; John Parson and John E. Jones are acquitted. The other prisoners are fined $100 each for resisting arrest (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). The new territorial governor, Stephen S. Harding, pardons them all a few days later. May 1863Many Morrisites leave Utah under the protection of Patrick Edward Connor, commanding the District of Utah. On May 5 a party of 160 (53 families, seven single men, and four widows) sets out with a company of California Volunteers; it reaches Soda Springs on May 20, where Connor has a town site surveyed on the north bank of the Bear River beside a new military post, Camp Connor (established by order of May 23). The Morrisites call their town Morristown. Connor also gives 150 Morrisites passage to Carson City, Nevada, in an empty supply train. Others settle in California. (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, Official Records, ser. 1, vol. 50, pt. 1, 226–29.) 1860s–Some Morrisites return to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, in Utah and elsewhere. The 2006 monument at South Weber notes that a few were rebaptized and remained there. Others find a home in the Reorganized Church (RLDS): the former Morrisite apostle Mark Hill Forscutt joins it in Salt Lake City in 1865, and John L. Bear (Johann Lebrecht Bär, 1838–1919), a Swiss convert from Affoltern am Albis who emigrated from Zürich in 1860 and lost his wife and child at Kington Fort, later serves as an RLDS missionary to Switzerland and Germany, dies in Independence, Missouri, and publishes his autobiography in the RLDS Journal of History. In 1865 RLDS missionaries at Malad, Idaho, baptize several people who appear on the roll. Others join only after years in the Morrisite groups: Erick and Caroline Eliason are baptized together at Soda Springs on June 9, 1870; Margaretta Cook leaves the Morrisites in Nevada in 1870 and is baptized RLDS in 1873; and Lena Hanson, at Soda Springs and then Deer Lodge, in 1895 (see the roll).

t: 1867–1881William W. Davies leads a Morrisite offshoot, the Kingdom of …
s: 1867–1881William W. Davies leads a Morrisite offshoot, the Kingdom of Heaven, near Walla Walla, Washington. He declares his infant son Arthur to be Christ returned, the “Walla Walla Jesus.” Lawsuits by former members end the community: in 1881 a court awards three of them $3,225, and the sheriff sells the community’s livestock and its eighty acres to satisfy the judgment. 1869Danish-language congregations keep membership and account books in Omaha, Nebraska, and Council Bluffs, Iowa.

t: 1870sMany members regather in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, under Ge…
s: 1870sMany members regather in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, under George Williams, the “Prophet Cainan,” who claims to be Morris's successor. In 1874 the Montana church is divided into two stakes. A local history of Anaconda dates the first Morrisite settlers in the valley to 1863, among them William Price Thomas on Warm Springs Creek, east of the later townsite; has a group under William James arriving in 1867 as others left; and describes a caravan of thirteen covered wagons that came in June 1871, part of a larger migration from Iowa, Nebraska, Utah and Idaho: Scandinavian families, mostly Danes, with English, Scottish and Welsh believers. It places the two congregations in the upper valley near Lost Creek and near Race Track Creek, with about eighty members in all (Patrick F. Morris, Anaconda, Montana, 1997, pp. 15–17). 1877Montana Morrisites begin building a wood-frame church a mile or so below Racetrack, south of Deer Lodge. 1879Robert T. Burton, indicted in 1870 for the killing of Isabella Bowman during the surrender, is tried and acquitted. Jan 1879George Williams prophesies that Deer Lodge County will be the site of the Second Coming. 1880In Chicago, Mark Hill Forscutt, a former Morrisite apostle now serving as an RLDS minister, baptizes James Brighouse (August 5) and confirms him (August 8), having baptized Mrs. Brighouse in July and preached the funeral of their infant child. In December Forscutt nominates Brighouse as a teacher in the branch. (Forscutt journal, 1880–1881, Vault MSS 811.) Four years later Brighouse founds the Order of Enoch.

t: 1882Williams dies, and the movement splits among rival successors. In …
s: 1882Williams dies, and the movement splits among rival successors. In Montana, where the church is known as the Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High, William James, its local president under Williams, is sustained in May 1882 over opposition, with Andrew Hendrikson and John R. Eardley as counselors. (Eardley, later a stake president, leaves Montana about 1900.) George Dove leads the California congregation. 1884A later claimant. James Brighouse, breaking from the RLDS Church, organizes the Order of Enoch in Independence, Missouri, a small commune with Lars Peterson whose main tenet is celibacy. After breaking with the Petersons and returning to Utah he proclaims himself the embodiment of the Second Coming and the “One Mighty and Strong,” and only then, as far as Kirk Watson can tell, teaches reincarnation. Brighouse had been brought into the RLDS Church in 1880 by the former Morrisite apostle Mark Hill Forscutt (see 1880), but Forscutt opposed the doctrine, calling it Morris’s “strange theory of repeated embodiment” (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702, p. 12). Watson, who has researched Brighouse, has found no connection between him and the Morrisites beyond shared ideas and language, and notes that the two men meant different things by the “seventh angel”: for Morris a stage in the soul’s ascent through the angelic ranks, for Brighouse a figure taken from Revelation 11. Watson also points out that the title was in Latter-day Saint use before either man took it up. The 1832 revelation now Doctrine and Covenants 88:112 speaks of “Michael, the seventh angel, even the archangel,” and in his funeral sermon for Joseph and Hyrum Smith in 1844, W. W. Phelps cast Joseph as the angel who would pour out the “vials of wrath,” an allusion to the seventh angel of Revelation 16; Latter-day Saints of the time often saw their prophet as the Seventh Angel (Kirk Watson, correspondence with the editor, November 2026, following Christopher James Blythe, “‘Would to God, Brethren, I Could Tell You Who I Am!’” Nova Religio 18, no. 2 (2014): 18–19; Phelps’s sermon as reconstructed in 1855, in Van Wagoner and Walker, “The Joseph/Hyrum Smith Funeral Sermon,” BYU Studies 23, no. 1 (1983): 15–16). One online account (Lost Mormonism) says the Order honored Morris as a prophet and martyr, but the standard references do not: Shields’s entry on the Order (Divergent Paths, 5th ed., §5.4) and Kraut’s note on Brighouse both omit Morris. Wikipedia describes the Order as the one Morrisite-related body that survived 1969; its later activity has not been confirmed for this guide.

t: 1886At a court meeting in the Lord’s House at Race Track, Montana, on …
s: 1886At a court meeting in the Lord’s House at Race Track, Montana, on May 10, George Thompson of London is elected president of the church; eleven members who decline to sustain him are given thirty days to do so. Thompson is probably the last general president. Andrew Hendrikson, a Danish immigrant who was never a Latter-day Saint, presides over the Montana Morrisites from 1886 until his death on July 3, 1921. 1886The Spirit Prevails, a collection of Morris's revelations, articles, and letters, is published by George S. Dove & Company. 1892In San Francisco, James Dove publishes A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites for the California congregation.

t: 1981–1988C. LeRoy Anderson publishes For Christ Will Come Tomorrow (19…
s: 1981–1988C. LeRoy Anderson publishes For Christ Will Come Tomorrow (1981) and Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites (1988), the first book-length histories. 1990A later claimant. Neal Chase, interpreter for Leland Jensen’s Missoula-based sect, the Bahá’ís Under the Provisions of the Covenant, publishes Ezekiel’s Temple in Montana. Drawing on Anderson’s book, he cites George Williams’s prophecy that Christ would come in the Deer Lodge Valley, identifies the Montana State Prison at Deer Lodge (where Jensen was held from 1969) as Ezekiel’s temple, and dates the fulfillment to August 9, 1969, Jensen’s first full day in prison. Anderson rejected this reading, noting that Williams named no date. The sect was not Morrisite in origin; it adopted Morrisite prophecies as confirmation of its leader’s mission. 1996–2010After Jensen’s death in 1996 the sect divides over leadership, with Chase leading one faction; lawsuits continue to about 2010.

July 2012Descendants of Morrisite families hold a reunion in Deer Lodge; the property owners allow them to visit the Racetrack church. 2026Kirk Watson publishes The Morrisites: Writings and Revelations, collecting writings of Morris, Williams, Davies, and the Doves. The Racetrack church still stands, in declining condition (see the condition record under Images).
History
Places Sites connected with the movement, and what can be seen at each today. MO-IMG-001 · Monument, December 2008

Kington Fort South Weber, Utah Built in 1853 and abandoned in 1858, then reoccupied by the Morrisites. Nothing of the fort survives; a monument to the Kington Fort–Morrisite War site, Sons of Utah Pioneers marker no. 128, was erected in August 2006 at 6600 South and 475 East (N 41.14677, W 111.96884), sponsored by the South Weber chapter of the Daughters of Utah Pioneers, the Ogden Pioneer chapter of the Sons of Utah Pioneers and All Build Construction and Landscaping, with the site designed by Douglas B. Stephens (Barlow, 2022). The fort was named for Bishop Thomas Kington, and “Kington” is the correct spelling. The monument itself notes that the earliest sources (the notebook kept by Kington’s wife, his gravestone, Wilford Woodruff’s journals, and early church records) all spell it that way; recent scholarship such as Holley (2008) follows them. Many nineteenth- and twentieth-century accounts, and some modern references, including the Utah History Encyclopedia and Wikipedia, write “Kingston Fort.” Insiders used both: Forscutt, who lived in the fort, wrote “Kingston’s Fort” and called it “the proper name” of the place (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702). Search under both spellings. A log cabin nearby, which the local historian Ed Cooper, from oral accounts of older South Weber residents, identified as the building Morris used to hold the three departing members whose detention led to the siege, is shown in MO-IMG-046–049; it has been moved from its original site, and the identification rests on local tradition. About 200 yards south, on the west side of the road, in the South Weber Pioneer Cemetery, a marker reads “Joseph Werner, ‘Morrisite,’ about 1870” (MO-IMG-021). The name lingered locally. In the early 2000s, while the editor was going door to door in South Weber, a woman then in her sixties said that elementary-school classmates had called her “Morrisite” as a taunt because of where in South Weber she lived; she said her family had no Morrisite connection. (Editor’s memorandum of recollection, written November 1, 2026; the conversation was not recorded at the time.) A cannonball from the siege was kept by the family of Al Peek, together with a portrait of Mary Christoffersen Anderson (MO-IMG-051–053; the portrait is MO-IMG-062). VisitThe monument is public. The Pioneer Cemetery appears to lie on private land but is reached by a public easement; stay on the access route. The cabin is on private property. MO-IMG-061 · Anderson gravestone, October 2018

Morristown Soda Springs, Idaho The Morrisites were among the founders of Soda Springs, one of the oldest towns in Idaho. Connor reported bringing 160 settlers (53 families, seven single men, and four widows), who arrived May 20, 1863, and were given building lots on a town site surveyed on the north bank of the Bear River, beside the military reservation of Camp Connor (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, OR). A later marker describes a 200-acre survey west of Soda Creek, lots of 25 by 130 feet, and one-room log homes with dirt floors. The Morrisite “Lower Town” stood below the military “Upper Town”; Soda Springs was the first seat of Oneida County, 1864–66. After the troops left in 1865, hard winters and failed crops thinned the settlement. Many Morrisites moved on, some north to the Blackfoot area, and others sold to miners and to Latter-day Saint settlers, whose new town site dates from Brigham Young’s visit of 1870–71. Most of the old town now lies under Alexander Reservoir. Those who stayed, led by Niels Anderson, carried their quarrel with the Mormon hierarchy into territorial politics; the Niels Anderson Homestead marker credits his anti-polygamy campaign with helping deny Mormons the vote in Idaho. Accounts differ on some details: most give 160 settlers (one popular account says about 325), Camp Connor’s founding is dated May 20 or May 23, and the National Park Service marker wrongly calls Morris Welsh-born. Markers stand in town, including the Park Service’s Morrisite settlement marker in the parking lot of a Latter-day Saint meetinghouse (HMDB), the state’s Camp Connor marker (HMDB), and “Law & Order on the Frontier” on Camp Connor’s probable site near the hospital (HMDB). Descendants held a reunion in Soda Springs on August 3, 2013. Niels and Mary Christoffersen Anderson, married at Morristown on July 20, 1863 (the date on their gravestone; some accounts give July 30), are buried in Fairview Cemetery at Soda Springs. Their gravestone carries a long bronze inscription giving a Morrisite account of the 1862 siege, in which Mary, then fourteen, lost her jaw to the first cannon shot fired into the fort. Forscutt, who was present, described her lower jaw “hanging only by a narrow strip of skin,” with two women dead beside her (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702; MO-IMG-061, with transcription; MO-IMG-062; HMDB; see also the Niels Anderson Homestead marker). VisitThe markers and the Anderson gravestone in Fairview Cemetery are publicly accessible. The townsite is largely under Alexander Reservoir.

Carson City & California Nevada · California The western congregations, where George Dove published The Spirit Prevails and led the California church after 1882. In May 1863 Connor gave 150 Morrisites passage to Carson City in an empty quartermaster’s train bound there for stores (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, OR). VisitNo surviving sites identified for this guide. Information welcome.

Omaha & Council Bluffs Nebraska · Iowa Danish-speaking congregations whose 1869 membership and account books survive in translation. VisitNo sites identified; the record survives in documents only. MO-IMG-014 · Racetrack church, November 2018

Deer Lodge Valley Powell and Deer Lodge counties, Montana The longest-lived center of the movement. The wood-frame Morrisite church, begun in 1877, still stands on private land at Racetrack, about 8 miles south of Deer Lodge: on the north side of Dempsey Road, just west of the railroad and the Interstate 90 frontage road (Exit 195; about 46.29° N, 112.75° W; NE¼ sec. 8, T6N R9W, Powell County). The county lists it as a frame building of 18 by 36 feet (Montana Cadastral, Montana State Library, consulted November 6, 2026). It was last photographed for this guide in November 2018. Called the Lord’s House, as the panel over its doors reads, it was the church’s meeting place: George Thompson was elected president of the church there in 1886, and Andrew Hendrikson (1886–1921) and George Johnson (1921–1954) presided over the Montana church from it. It is the only Morrisite church building known to survive, and its condition has worsened markedly since 2009. See the condition record under Images. View onlyThe church is privately owned, unsafe and not open to the public. View it from Dempsey Road or the frontage road; do not enter the property.

Kingdom of Heaven Walla Walla, Washington William W. Davies's commune near Walla Walla, 1867–1881. Its site lay on the west side of Mormon Grade Road, a few hundred yards south of Scenic Loop Road, near Russell Creek (Dan Clark, Walla Walla 2020, correspondence with the editor, November 2026). An interpretive sign that Walla Walla 2020 put up at the corner of Scenic Loop and Mormon Grade roads was shot up, replaced, shot up again and finally stolen. The road name and Davies’s grave in Lyons Cemetery remain. VisitLyons Cemetery is public. The colony site is not marked.

t: Cilley, Evans and Courtney v. Davies, 1880

Davies, 1880 Frontier Justice WAL-3153 Held by Washington State Archives, Eastern Region Branch, Cheney, Washington Contents Case file of the Washington Territorial District Court for Walla Walla County, original case no. 2373, 1880: a civil suit to collect wages and debts brought by Asa B. Cilley, Thomas W. Evans and A. J. Courtney against William W. Davies, Alfred Davies and W. Wood. The archives’ index calls it the “Walla Walla Jesus” case. The file runs to 292 pages. It holds depositions taken before a referee in 1880–81 by members and former members, among them Peter C. Klemgaard, Swen O. Hagg and Broer Sorenson of the 1861–62 roll, and Davies himself; a list of the forty-three members in March 1881, with their ages; printed tracts, hymns and letters by Davies filed as exhibits, among them his printed “Synopsis of Remarks” at a meeting of January 2, 1876; lists of donations to the community from 1866 to 1878; the referee’s report; the judgment of May 25, 1881, for $3,225 (Evans $2,700, Courtney $400, Cilley $125), with interest and costs; and the sheriff’s returns: Davies’s livestock and equipment were sold on June 11, 1881, and the community’s eighty acres, the west half of the northwest quarter of section 34, township 7 north, range 37 east, on July 16, 1881. Related case First National Bank of Walla Walla v. William A. Davies, William W. Davies and Lewis H. Bowman, 1885 (WAL-4626, original no. 4262; 28 pages): nine promissory notes of November 14, 1879, totaling $1,770, made by William W. Davies and his son William A. Davies to Lewis H. Bowman, who sold them to the bank the same day. The bank sued in February 1885 and took judgment by default on May 21, 1885, for $4,141.60 with attorney’s fees. The son was served in Lincoln County, near Sprague. Access Indexed in “Frontier Justice,” the Washington State Archives’ guide to the territorial court case files, 1853–1889 (index record, 1880; 1885). The papers are not online; copies may be ordered from the Eastern Region Branch, which scanned both files for this guide in November 2026. Pages 158–195, the depositions of five defense witnesses, were missing when the county microfilmed the file; Whitman College Library later found them among its own holdings and returned them, and they are now with the case file (notes by the Walla Walla County clerk and by the archivist, 2002, filed with the case). Pages 133–157 were not among the scans received. Kirk Watson’s edition prints Davies’s own deposition in the 1880 case.

“Third District Territorial Court,” April 1, 1863 Deseret News, p. 4 What it is The court’s own report of the March 1863 term at Salt Lake City, Chief Justice Kinney presiding, in which the Morrisites taken at Kington Fort were tried. It names the seven convicted of murder, whom the Morrisites’ own histories name differently, and the eighty-five men tried for resisting an officer. The murder trial In People v. Peter Klemgard and others, for the deaths of the two posse men, the prosecutor entered a nolle prosequi for Richard Cook. Robert T. Burton, Judson L. Stoddart, Theodore McKean, David J. Ross and James Hales testified for the prosecution; Margaret Cook, Jens Christian Sorensen, Mrs. Dove, James Bowman, Joseph Marsh, James Mather, Mrs. Banks, David Thomas, Mrs. Gray, John O. Mather, Mrs. Garrett, Philip Hewit, Peter Swenson and Lebrecht Bar for the defence. On Friday, March 27, the jury found Peter Klemgard, Christian Neilsen, Abraham Taylor, Kadrup Neilsen, Jens Christiansen, Andrew Lee and Andrew M. Mason guilty of murder in the second degree, and John Parsons and John E. Jones not guilty. The sentences were fifteen years at hard labor for Klemgard, twelve for Neilsen and ten for each of the others. On Saturday Richard Cook, John Parsons and John E. Jones pleaded guilty to resisting an officer and were fined $100 each, and Cook’s $50 fine for contempt in June 1862 was remitted. Two lists of the seven The Spirit Prevails (p. 7) and Eardley’s Gems (p. 31) name the seven as Peter C. Klemgard, John Nielson, Abraham Taylor, George Lee, Christian Nelsen, Jens Christiansen and John E. Jones. The court report agrees on four, but has Kadrup Neilsen, Andrew Lee and Andrew M. Mason where they have John Nielson, George Lee and John E. Jones, and it records John E. Jones as acquitted. The report was printed within days of the verdict, and its sentences (fifteen, twelve and five of ten years) agree with Stenhouse; the Morrisite accounts were written decades later. Resisting an officer On Thursday, March 26, in the case of Peter L. McCue and others, the jury found the defendants guilty of resisting an officer and fined each $100. Chief Justice Kinney told them the court had been disposed to look with mercy on men who had acted under the direction of leaders they trusted. Of the eighty-five names called, sixty-eight match a man on the 1861–62 roll, nine more probably do, and eight are not on it (marked * below). t: Two revelations to the First Presidency, January 14 and 16, 1860
s: Two revelations to the First Presidency, January 14 and 16, 1860 Church History Library, CR 1234 1 What it is Two manuscript revelations, signed “Jesus Christ” and addressed to “the first presidency of the Church of Jesus Christ of Later day saints and all so to the twelve apostles.” Both demand that the leaders receive “my servant Joseph.” They are filed as anonymous letters among Brigham Young’s incoming correspondence for 1860, outside the folders of Morris’s revelations, and were identified by Kirk Watson in November 2026, after his edition of Morris’s letters was published, so they are not in it. Why they matter They are among the earliest dated revelations of Morris to survive in manuscript. The Spirit Prevails has only No. 2 (“Winter of 1859”) before them; its No. 3 is dated March 1860. Neither is printed there, but both are early forms of later texts. The January 14 revelation opens “when you whas small in your own eyes i took you and i rose you to the apostle ship,” the same opening as No. 18, “Revelation to President Brigham Young” (October 2, 1860). Like No. 18, it charges Young with turning the Lord’s servant away from his door and speaks of “the throne of isreal.” But it is addressed to the Twelve as well as to Young, and its warnings to them, which name Jeroboam, promise “fresh apostles” in their place and threaten to cut them off root and branch, are not in No. 18, which is addressed to Young alone. The January 16 revelation requires anyone with “gould and silver and houses and lands and whives” to “lay them at the feet of my servant Joseph,” the test Morris set out again in No. 185 (December 28, 1861). How they were received The office docket on the January 14 letter reads “Jan 14 1860 / Balderdash / About revelations / Rec Jan 20 1860,” and the same clerk wrote “Balderdash” above the heading of each revelation. The letter is addressed “To president Brigham Young grait Sault Lake City.” The hand Kirk Watson, who has transcribed many of Morris’s writings, identifies the hand and spelling as Morris’s. He compared the January 14 revelation with a revelation “to president young” dated October 11, 1858, catalogued as a “Joseph Morris letter” in the folder “Revelations of Joseph Morris, 1858–1860” of the same office files. The two share the same dating formula (“October the 11 1858,” “January the 14 1860”), the same letter forms and the same phonetic spelling (“speckelating,” “whas”). Read it January 14, 1860 (5 images) · January 16, 1860 (2 images). t: MO-IMG-032The slough below the bluffs. Kington Fort stood on the Weber…
s: MO-IMG-032The slough below the bluffs. Kington Fort stood on the Weber River flood plain, in a bowl ringed on the south and west by sandy bluffs about half a mile off and some two hundred feet high. On June 13, 1862, the posse took its position on the bluffs south of the fort, from which it could see into the fort (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 64, 112, 128). The plan of the fort drawn by G. Q. Jones for the Sons of Utah Pioneers (1996) marks a slough just outside the south gate, and its notes say that on June 15 an armored battery made from the rear of a wagon was rolled toward the fort, caught a wheel in the mud and tipped over, and that its crew retreated under musket fire. Jones does not give his source, and Anderson describes the rolling battery as pushed up to the fort wall (p. 135). The editor, from Jones’s plan and the comments of the South Weber historian Ed Cooper on a visit to the site, takes this to be the slough where the battery mired. See the map on the Kington Fort page.South Weber, Utah · before February 2004 (scanned print)

Transcription of the Anderson plaque (MO-IMG-061) NIELS ANDERSON · OCTOBER 3 [?], 1835 – MARCH 4 [?], 1926 MARY CHRISTOFFERSEN ANDERSON · JULY 26, 1847 – JULY 13 [?], 1928 THEY WERE BORN IN DENMARK; JOINED THE MORMONS THERE. IN 1857 MRS. ANDERSON ARRIVED AT BURLINGTON, IOWA; DETAINED THERE UNTIL 1859 ON ACCOUNT OF JOHNSTON’S ARMY HAVING TO BE SENT TO UTAH. THAT YEAR SHE WALKED NEARLY ALL THE WAY TO SALT LAKE CITY. IN 1860 MR. ANDERSON CAME; HE PULLED A HAND-CART FROM FLORENCE, NEBRASKA. THEY SOON SAW THE DECEPTION IN “BRIGHAMISM,” JOINED MORRIS A SECEDER FROM BRIGHAM. MAY 22 [?], 1863, THEY CAME TO SODA SPRINGS WITH THE FIRST SETTLERS; THEY WERE ESCORTED AND PROTECTED BY GEN. CONNOR AND CALIFORNIA VOLUNTEERS. JULY 20, 1863, THEY WERE MARRIED HERE; THEIR MARRIAGE WAS THE FIRST IN IDAHO TERRITORY AS FAR AS THEY KNEW. LATER MR. ANDERSON BECAME “THE FATHER OF THE ANTI-MORMON PARTY” IN IDAHO. AT SOUTH WEBER, UTAH, JUNE 13–15, 1862, MR. AND MRS. ANDERSON WERE IN “THE MORRISITE MASSACRE.” MRS. ANDERSON’S CHIN WAS SHOT AWAY WITH A CANNON BALL, THAT KILLED MRS. BARBARA DE[…]THELM [?] AND MRS. JOSEPH (?) MARSH, FIRED BY GEN. ROBERT T. BURTON’S MORMON MILITIA INTO A BOWERY OF UNARMED “MORRISITES,” JUNE 13, BECAUSE THEY REFUSED TO OBEY “BRIGHAM’S” DECREES, AFTER JOHNSTON’S ARMY HAD LEFT UTAH ON ACCOUNT OF THE CIVIL WAR. MRS. J. L. BEAR AND HER BABY WERE KILLED WITH ANOTHER CANNON BALL. THEN MANY MORRISITES WITH THEIR OLD GUNS TRIED RESISTANCE. ON THE THIRD DAY ALL SURRENDERED UNDER A WHITE FLAG. MRS. ANDERSON SAYS: “WHEN MORRIS CAME BEFORE GEN. BURTON, THE LATTER USED ABUSIVE LANGUAGE AND TRIED TO RIDE OVER MORRIS ON HIS HORSE. THIS ABUSE WAS ON ACCOUNT OF HIS RELIGIOUS TEACHING. I SAW HIM … SHOOT MORRIS.” DOW’S AFFIDAVIT SAYS: BURTON SHOT MORRIS, BANKS, MRS. JAMES BOWMAN AND ANOTHER WOMAN, AFTER THEY SURRENDERED. TEN “MORRISITES” WERE KILLED, AND ONE “MORMON.” THE PRISONERS WERE TO BE TRIED AT THE NEXT TERM OF COURT HELD BY CHIEF JUSTICE KINNEY, A MORMON. IN THE MEANTIME GOV. HARDING, ASSOCIATE JUSTICES WAITE, DRAKE, COL. CONNOR AND VOLUNTEERS ARRIVED. “SEVEN MORRISITES” WERE SENTENCED TO IMPRISONMENT FROM “TEN TO FIFTEEN YEARS.” “SIXTY-SIX” HEAVILY FINED. “WE,” WROTE GOV. HARDING IN 1874, “ATTENDED THROUGH THE TRIAL, WHICH WAS NOTHING BUT A MOCKERY. BURTON ADMITTED HIS SHOOTING THE PRISONERS. … HAD I BEEN ON THE BENCH I SHOULD HAVE HAD HIM ARRESTED … ; BUT IT WOULD HAVE BEEN USELESS. THE JURORS WOULD ALL BE MORMONS, AND RECOGNIZE NO LAW BUT ‘THE COMMANDS OF AUTHORITY.’ “PETITIONS WERE GOTTEN UP FOR THE UNCONDITIONAL PARDON OF THE MORRISITES, WHICH WERE SIGNED BY ALL THE GENTILES, … NOT A MORMON SIGNED THEM. … “I ISSUED THE PARDON; … SOME MOUNTED MORTARS … COMMANDING THE BEE-HIVE HOUSE AND LION HOUSE, MADE THINGS TOLERABLY SMOOTH ON THE SURFACE.” BRIGHAM YOUNG JUNE 15, AS BY H. P. McLANE, SAID, “THAT MORRIS AND BANKS WILL BE TAKEN I HAVE NO DOUBT. … BUT IF I HAD MY OWN WAY ABOUT IT, I WOULD NOT SPARE NEITHER MAN, WOMAN NOR CHILD; BUT AS IT IS A UNITED STATES AFFAIR, THEY CAN HAVE IT AS THEY PLEASE. BUT AS REGARDS THIS YOUNG MAN, HE HAS DIED A MARTYR TO THE CAUSE AND KINGDOM OF OUR GOD. … THIS WAS A MATTER OF NECESSITY. … THE WORST … I [?] DISLIKE … , IS THAT AFTER THEY ARE ROUTED, THE … ACCURSED DEVILS … WILL BE TRYING TO SNEAK BACK INTO THE CHURCH AGAIN. …” R. W. YOUNG WRITING FOR THE “CONTRIBUTOR,” OF 1890, FOR THE MORMON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION SAYS: “THE … ACTION OF THE GOVERNOR WAS FOLLOWED … IN COURSE OF TIME, BY PERSECUTION OF GEN. BURTON. … A GRAND JURY WAS LED IN … 1870, TO BRING IN AN INDICTMENT FOR MURDER … , AND … (HE) THOUGHT HIMSELF COMPELLED BY CIRCUMSTANCES TO EVADE ARREST … LATER, ANOTHER INDICTMENT WAS FOUND AGAINST GEN. BURTON … , HE MADE NO ATTEMPT TO ESCAPE. …” BETWEEN THESE TWO INDICTMENTS A RULING HAD “PROVIDED IN SUBSTANCE FOR JURIES HALF MORMON, AND HALF GENTILE.” THIS YOUNG SAYS, “THE PROSECUTION LABORED LONG, AND,” “CLOUDS OF WITNESSES WERE BROUGHT FORTH,” “TO PERSUADE THE JURY,” “ONE-HALF BEING NON-MORMONS,” THAT BURTON KILLED MRS. BOWMAN. THIS CASE WAS NO. 3109, U.S. VS. BURTON FOR “MURDER 1ST DEGREE,” SET FOR TRIAL 1ST DAY OF FEB. TERM 1879, MARCH 8 — INDICTMENT DISMISSED. THIS WAS ONE OF THE THREE INDICTMENTS AGAINST HIM. IT WAS ASKED: WHAT ABOUT THE CASE FOR KILLING MORRIS? U.S. DISTRICT ATTORNEY VANZILE ANSWERED “WHAT IS THE USE, IF THEY WILL NOT CONVICT FOR KILLING AN INNOCENT WOMAN?” TO FATHER AND MOTHER, AND HISTORIC TO MAN, WE DEDICATE THIS MEMORIAL. ABRAHAM CHRISTOPHER ANDERSON, I[D]A COLLETT, ANNA CHRISTINA ROGERS, DAVID ANDREW ANDERSON, ABELONE LARSEN, PETER WILLIAM ANDERSON, NIELS CHRISTIAN ANDERSON, MARY AMELIA VERHAM. Transcribed by the editor from MO-IMG-061 (October 2018), keeping the plaque’s capitals and punctuation; paragraphs follow its indentations. Ellipses and the “(?)” after “Joseph” are on the plaque. Bracketed readings are the editor’s and are uncertain where the bronze is worn: the dates marked [?], the first victim’s surname (perhaps the Swiss name Diethelm), and Ida Collett’s first name. The plaque is the Anderson children’s account and quotes its sources selectively; compare the trial record and the histories in the Bibliography. Corrections from a clearer reading are welcome. About this roll Roll of Membership: Names of Persons Baptized into the Fulness of the Gospel USHS PAM 9569c1 Published San Francisco: Geo. S. Dove & Co., May 1886. 8 pp. Subtitle: “Names of persons baptized during the administration of Joseph Morris, at South Weber, Utah Territory, in the years of 1861 and 1862.” Copy Utah History Information Center (Utah State Historical Society), Salt Lake City, PAM 9569c1; gift of William Mulder. Larson’s transcription also records the words “Reorganized Church Library,” probably a library mark on the copy. Compiler’s note “All the names that we found in the record book are in this list. We feel assured that there were many persons baptized whose names were not recorded.” Absence from the roll does not show that someone was not a member. Pencil notes In the copy Larson transcribed, someone has totaled the names in pencil at 430 and marked the church’s officers (listed above); a further pencil note reads “174 Scan names,” apparently a count of Scandinavian names. The roll has 430 names, matching that total; Larson’s transcription had left out David Thomas (note 10). This transcription Made from David A. Larson’s transcription of the Utah State Historical Society copy (MORRISITES-L mailing list, RootsWeb, March 25, 2007), then checked name by name on November 2, 2026, against a photocopy of the printed pamphlet in the editor’s files. The check restored one name (David Thomas) and corrected fourteen spellings to match the print. Names follow the order and spelling of the roll; where a name repeats, the roll adds “2.” Notes on doubtful readings are numbered. Hover over a link to see the basis for the identification and who supplied it. Links open FamilySearch’s public page for the person, which needs no sign-in; a free account shows the full record and its sources. Family Tree is open to editing by anyone, so check those sources before relying on it. What counts A shared name is not enough. A match needs something tying the person to the Morrisites or to South Weber in 1861–62, or a name rare enough in Utah Territory then to leave no other candidate. Matches that rest on circumstantial evidence, such as a husband and wife both on the roll and a likely place, or a family whose members on the roll all match one family in Family Tree, are linked but marked “probable”; corrections are welcome. Cases with more than one candidate are explained in the notes instead. Contribute If you can identify someone, send the FamilySearch ID and your evidence to contact@morrisite.org. Contributions are credited. Families on the roll Updated as evidence is added What it shows People on the roll who were related by birth or marriage, grouped by family, with the places they lived after 1862. The groups come from Family Tree, membership records and published histories; a relationship that rests only on a likely guess is left out until it is checked. Many Morrisite families stayed together after the siege and married into one another at Soda Springs, Deer Lodge and in the Carson Valley, so a descendant of one family may find related families in the same group. Contribute If you know of a connection that is not shown, write to contact@morrisite.org. What became of them Updated as evidence is added How it is counted Each person counts as “not yet known” until a source shows where he or she went: the RLDS Church (Reorganized Church, now Community of Christ), back to the LDS Church, one of the later Morrisite groups in Idaho, Montana, Nevada, California, Washington Territory or Iowa, or death at Kington Fort during the siege of June 13–15, 1862. Many Morrisites joined the RLDS Church only after years in the groups at Soda Springs, Deer Lodge, Carson Valley or Walla Walla; when a source shows both stages, the person is counted as “stayed Morrisite, later joined the RLDS Church,” with a half-green, half-blue dot. The sources are RLDS and LDS membership records, FamilySearch, and published histories. Where the source names someone who is probably, but not certainly, the person on the roll, the evidence begins “Probable identification.” A colored dot beside a name shows the category; hover over it, or tap it on a phone, for the evidence. Send additions or corrections to contact@morrisite.org. Reading the roll Spellings vary, especially for Danish and Swedish names: search under Hanson and Hansen, Peterson and Petersen, Christiansen and Christensen, Sorenson and Sorensen. The roll itself spells some families two ways (Peterson and Petersen; Lorensen and Lorentzen). The roll records baptisms in 1861–62. It does not show who remained in the church, who left before the siege of June 1862, or who later joined the Soda Springs, Carson Valley, Walla Walla, or Montana groups. Later rolls, including those of the Montana church, which existed until 1969, are cited in Repositories but not published here.

Paths into the movement What brought Latter-day Saints to Joseph Morris? The members left few accounts of their reasons, so this section tests what the records can show: when people reached Utah, whom they crossed the plains with, where they came from, and whether they joined as families. Companies are known for 98 of the 164 people linked to Family Tree, from the Mormon Pioneer Overland Travel records attached there and from the rosters of the Church History Biographical Database (CHD). These are associations in the records, not reasons the members gave. When they came, against everyone who came 1847–51 0.5 1852 0.5 1853 3.9 1854 3.3 1855 5.3 1856 4.5 1857–58 1.1 1859 11.2 1860 7.3 1861 0.0 Roll members per 1,000 people in the CHD’s pioneer companies of each year. The highest rate is 1859 (18 of 1,606). People who had arrived in 1859 and 1860, a year or two before Morris began baptizing, joined about twice as often as those who came in 1853–56, and far more often than those who came before 1853. Those who arrived in 1861 had little time to join before the roll closed. CHD counts are the names it holds, not every emigrant; the roll members identified so far are not a random sample, and some were found by searching these same rosters. Crossing together Robert F. Weighing the factors Factor What the records show How far it goes Recent arrival 63 of 117 identified people with a year of arrival reached Utah in 1856 or later; the rate per 1,000 emigrants peaks in 1859. Strong pattern, the clearest in the records. Why newcomers joined more often (fewer ties to their wards, less property, hardship on arrival) is not yet measured. Crossing together 65 of 98 with a known company shared it with another roll family. Moderate. It overlaps with origin and with how the names were found. Language and origin 168 of 430 names on the roll are Scandinavian. Strong for the roll as a whole, but it overlaps with arrival year; how it compares with the population of Utah in 1861 has not been measured. Family 127 roll names belong to the 30 family groups found so far (see the roll). Strong where known: families often joined together, so one household’s decision accounts for several names. Many relationships on the roll are still unfound. Place 57 of the 91 roll members found in the 1860 census lived in Davis or Weber County, near South Weber. Strong but expected: Morris preached and baptized there. Leaders and wards The South Weber bishop, Richard Cook, and his brother John joined; sixteen were cut off together on February 11, 1861. Not counted. Followed through the roll notes and person pages. The factors overlap: a Danish family who crossed in 1859 and settled near South Weber counts under four of them at once, so they cannot be added up. A fair reading is that Morris drew most on recent emigrants, Danish and British, who came as families and lived near him, and least on Saints settled since the early 1850s.

Open questions

Questions for research Questions the guide has not been able to settle, for students, local historians, and other researchers. Questions of record can be advanced with records that are digitized or held in Utah, Idaho, Montana, or California. Questions of interpretation ask what the movement means for the history of religion; they suit theses and articles. If you take one up, or can answer one, write to contact@morrisite.org. Answers will be credited here. The edition of Forscutt’s “Sketch of Joseph Morris” is in progress by the editor. Questions of record Where is Joseph Morris buried? Open Known The Salt Lake City Cemetery sexton’s record lists Morris under June 15, 1862, as no. 1469; the entry just before his, no. 1468, is Peter Wahler of the posse, written “Walden” (see “Did one posse member die, or two?” below). Morris lies in the pauper ground, in an unmarked grave. A tradition holds that he was buried beneath a street so that he would be trodden underfoot; no published source for it has been found. Where to look Salt Lake City Cemetery office (plat maps of the pauper sections); sexton’s records on FamilySearch; Salt Lake newspapers for June 1862 in Utah Digital Newspapers; where the tradition first appears in print or family accounts. Did Brigham Young ever answer Morris? Open Known About a dozen of Morris’s letters survive in Young’s office files (CR 1234 1). Anderson found no reply, and reports a penciled note on the first letter, “He’s weak minded.” Two more Morris texts, revelations dated January 14 and 16, 1860, were found in 2026 filed as anonymous letters; a clerk docketed them “Balderdash” and received them January 20, 1860, and the first charges Young with turning the Lord’s servant away from his door (Documents). That docket is so far the only recorded reaction from the office. Kirk Watson’s edition transcribes twelve of the letters, October 11, 1858, to November 26, 1860, with catalog links (dated list on the Documents page); others may be catalogued as anonymous. Where to look Young’s letterpress copybooks and office journals, 1857–1861, in the same collection; the Journal of Wilford Woodruff for February 1861; the anonymous letters in the same files. What did Joseph F. Smith write to Niels Anderson? Open Known In 1903 Niels Anderson asked the church to help his wife, Mary Christoffersen Anderson, whose jaw was shot away in 1862. His letters survive (CR 1 191, digitized), and they answer a letter from Smith dated February 25, 1903, which is not in the file. Whether any help followed is unknown. Where to look Joseph F. Smith and First Presidency letterpress copybooks for 1903; Bannock Stake and Soda Springs ward records. Who were the Morrisites? In progress Known The roll of membership printed in 1886 lists 430 people baptized at South Weber in 1861–62. Since November 2026 this guide has linked 164 of them to FamilySearch Family Tree, marked 81 men named among the prisoners of June 1862, recorded the later path of 59, grouped families, and begun pages on individual members (for example John Parson and Erik Eliasson). Counts of sex, origin, age and birthplace are on Who they were. Most members are still known only by name, and the identifications marked probable need checking. Where to look The roll; Slaterville and other ward records; the 1860 and 1870 censuses; Soda Springs, Carson Valley, and Deer Lodge records; Black, Early Members of the Reorganized Church; descendants’ family records. Findings are added to the roll and person pages with their sources; living people are excluded. Who died at Kington Fort? Open Known Accounts differ on the number of dead and on some of their names and dates. The two posse deaths are now settled (Jared Smith and Peter Wahler; see below). On the Morrisite side, Morris was killed at the surrender and John Banks died in custody that evening; Forscutt saw two women dead from the first cannon shot on June 13, and Anne Bear and her infant were killed at the fort that day (roll notes, Bar, Labrach). The names of the other dead, and the date of each death, have not been checked against one another. No list checked against all the sources exists. Where to look Contemporary newspapers; Woodruff’s journal; the Journal History; Forscutt’s account; the Anderson gravestone; the Salt Lake City Cemetery sexton’s record, which has Morris and Wahler as nos. 1469 and 1468; Weber County burial records; the Deseret News of June 18, 1862 (Documents); testimony from the 1879 trial of Robert T. Burton. What became of the California congregation? Open Known George and James Dove led the church in San Francisco after 1882 and published its books into the 1890s. How and when the congregation ended is not known. Where to look San Francisco directories and newspapers in the California Digital Newspaper Collection; probate and cemetery records for the Dove family; the imprints of later Morrisite publications. What do the Danish revelations say? Open Known The USU collection holds a bound volume of Morris’s revelations in Danish that does not seem to exist anywhere else. It has not been translated or compared with The Spirit Prevails. Where to look USU Special Collections, Caine MSS 10. A reader of nineteenth-century Danish handwriting is needed. Where are the records of the 1863 trials? In progress Known At the March 1863 term, ten Morrisites were indicted for killing the two posse men: seven were convicted of second-degree murder, two were acquitted, and one case was dropped (nolle prosequi). One man was sentenced to fifteen years, one to twelve, and five to ten. Sixty-six others were fined $100 for resisting the posse (Fanny Stenhouse, An Englishwoman in Utah, 1880; Bancroft, History of Utah, ch. 22). Governor Harding pardoned them all a few days later; Anderson (Revisited, p. 145) says the proclamation named the convicted men, and Eardley says John Parson carried the pardon to the penitentiary (Gems, p. 31). t: Lee Pierce and the Walla Walla court files
s: Archivist · Washington State Archives Lee Pierce and the Walla Walla court files For decades the story in Walla Walla was that the court records of the lawsuits against William W. Davies had gone missing. A researcher who asked for them at the county courthouse was told they had been checked out, and he never found them. They were safe all along in the Washington State Archives, whose Eastern Region Branch in Cheney holds the territorial court records for most of the state’s eleven eastern counties. Lee Pierce, an archivist at the branch, answered the editor’s request the next morning with page counts and costs for both files, and the same afternoon he scanned and sent the whole 1885 bank suit and most of the 292-page 1880 case. He also supplied the archives’ preferred citation, so the files can be cited properly. They hold sworn testimony from men and women who lived in Davies’s community, printed tracts filed as exhibits, the lists of what members gave, the 1881 judgment and the sheriff’s sales, much of it new to this guide. See Repositories. Work like this rarely gets public credit, and guides like this one depend on it. Thank you, Lee.

t: How a descendant filled in the Eliason story
s: From the families How a descendant filled in the Eliason story Keith Chappelow, a descendant of Erik and Karin Eliasson, wrote to the editor with what his family knew. He sent the family’s account of the Eliasons at Soda Springs and Racetrack, pages from Joseph Smith III and the Restoration (1952), a family group sheet, and pages from a 1989 history of Powell County, Montana. That led to Family Tree links for Erik and Karin; their 1870 baptisms into the RLDS Church; their daughter Anna, whom an early county history calls the first white child born at Soda Springs; Erik’s brother Elias, who came to Soda Springs in 1863 but is not on the roll; and Joseph Smith III’s 1889 visit to the old camp at Weber with John Parson. See the pages on Erik and Karin. Is there a Morrisite in your family? Family accounts, letters, photographs, group sheets and local histories can answer questions no archive can. Share what you have; nothing is published without your permission.

From the community · local history groups What local history groups added In November the editor shared this guide in local history groups on Facebook in places where the Morrisites settled, beginning with Deer Lodge, Montana, and Walla Walla, Washington. Within a day the replies were changing the guide. Deer Lodge. A reader who once worked for a Soren Beck near Avon pointed the way to a 1902 biography of Soren R. Beck, who came to work on Niels R. Beck’s ranch in 1884 and was probably his nephew. A great-grandson of George Johnson, the last official leader of the Montana Morrisites, who preached at the Lord’s House near Racetrack until 1954, joined the conversation. So did descendants of families who built the church and worshiped there, neighbors who want to see it preserved, and a volunteer at the Deer Lodge County museum, which holds a pump organ said to have come from the Morrisites. Walla Walla. A reader asked whether the editor had checked Whitman College and recalled that the court records of the lawsuit against William W. Davies had gone missing from the county courthouse. Following up led to the case file in the Washington State Archives and to Whitman’s copies of depositions and an 1882 photograph of the Davies family and home. See Repositories. Thank you to everyone who has commented, shared and written. If your family or town has a Morrisite story, a photograph or an old record, share what you have. About

About this guide Where the material comes from, how it is checked, and how to cite it. How the guide was compiled The guide brings together work done over more than two decades. Its foundation is the research of C. LeRoy Anderson, whose files at Utah State University (Caine Coll. MSS 10) remain the largest body of Morrisite records. The editor assisted Anderson with the 2010 edition of his history and has studied the Morrisite apostle and later RLDS minister Mark Hill Forscutt since at least 2001, when his first article on Forscutt appeared, including transcribing Forscutt’s journals. Photographs of the sites were taken by the editor from the early 2000s onward. Kirk Watson’s 2026 edition of Morrisite writings, published scholarship, and records shared by descendants fill out the rest. Standards Citations follow The Chicago Manual of Style. Every work in the bibliography has been examined by the editor in at least one edition; where a page reference comes from an edition not seen, the entry says so. A work known only from another source’s citation will be marked Not yet checked. Facts are drawn from published works with citations; their text is not reproduced. Videos and photographs by others are linked, not copied, unless they have been shared for this guide; those are credited. Dates marked provisional, approximate, or “ca.” are flagged as such and revised when better evidence turns up. Membership rolls and other records naming private individuals are cited but not republished, with one exception: the 1861–62 South Weber roll, printed in 1886 and naming only people baptized more than 160 years ago, is given in full on the Roll of membership page. Changes are listed under What’s new. Oral and field sources Records of the editor’s own fieldwork, cited in this guide. Rogers, Eric Paul. “Memorandum of Recollection: South Weber Door-to-Door Visit.” Signed memorandum, November 1, 2026, recalling an unrecorded canvass of South Weber residents made before February 2004 in preparation for the editor’s 2006 John Whitmer Historical Association paper. PDF Privacy The guide counts visits with GoatCounter, an open-source service that uses no cookies and collects no personal information. It records which pages are read, how visitors arrived, and what words are typed into the search box, so the editor can see what readers look for and where the guide falls short. No one is tracked from one site to another, and the counts are not shared or sold. How to cite this guide Rogers, Eric Paul, ed. Morrisite.org: A Research Guide to the Morrisites. On the roll Erik Eliasson (1817–1893) A Swedish convert baptized into Joseph Morris’s Church of the Firstborn at South Weber, who stayed with the Morrisites at Soda Springs, joined the RLDS Church in 1870, and died among the Morrisite families of the Deer Lodge Valley. On the roll Eliason, Erick, in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886; listed with Eliason, Karen Born May 2, 1817, Västmanland, Sweden Died March 6, 1893, Racetrack, Deer Lodge Valley, Montana Wife Karin Caroline Anderson (1830–1902), on the roll as Eliason, Karen; married 1860 (FamilySearch LHN8-4C5) Children Six: Caroline (born 1861 at Farmington, Utah), then Anna, Joseph, the twins Jacob and John, and Isaac, all born at Soda Springs between 1863 and 1869 (Family Tree) Later path Stayed with the Morrisites, then joined the RLDS Church Family Tree FamilySearch MVRH-QQ6, Erik Eliasson (1817–1893) Life 2 May 1817Born in Västmanland, Sweden. (Family Tree) 1860Marries Karin Caroline Anderson, who reached Utah that year. (Family Tree) 1861–62Baptized with Karin into the Church of the Firstborn at South Weber; both names are on the roll of membership. His name is not on the list of men taken at Kington Fort and brought before Judge Kinney (Deseret News, June 25, 1862); whether he was at the fort in June 1862 is not known. May 1863Comes to Soda Springs with the Morrisites under General Connor’s escort. Shupe’s early list of those families names “Eric Eliason” and “Mrs. Caroline Eliason,” and also his brother Elias and Elias’s wife. (Shupe, p. 13) 2 Aug 1863Daughter Anna born at Soda Springs; Shupe calls her the first white child born there. (Shupe, p. 29; Family Tree) 1 Sep 1867Son John Eric born at Soda Springs. (family account) 9 Jun 1870Baptized into the RLDS Church at Soda Springs by Lars Edler, on the same day as Karin, who is entered as Caroline Eliasson, born March 7, 1830, in Sweden. (Black, vol. 2) After 1870Takes the twins, Jacob and John, to the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, leaving part of the family at Soda Springs, and settles on the ranch near Racetrack that his grandson still held in 1989. The grandson’s account gives 1868, but the twins were born in 1867 and Isaac at Soda Springs in 1869, so the move came later. (Powell County: Where It All Began, pp. 108–109) June 1880The census counts Erik three times: as a married farmer living alone in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana; as a rancher living alone at Soda Springs; and, as “Alexr. Eliasson,” 63, at the head of the family at Soda Springs with “Carrie,” 50, and all six children, including the thirteen-year-old twins. He was already working land in Montana while the family’s home was still at Soda Springs. (1880 U.S. census) 14 Jan 1888Receives the patent for his 40-acre homestead in the Deer Lodge Valley (Montana Principal Meridian, T6N R9W, sec. 4), Homestead Certificate 560 at the Helena land office. The Homestead Act required five years’ residence before final proof, so he was on the land by about 1882 at the latest. His son Joseph patented the adjoining 40 acres in 1889. (BLM General Land Office records) 1893Dies at Racetrack, Montana, on March 6. (Family Tree) Karin dies at Soda Springs in 1902. (Family Tree) His brother Elias Erik’s younger brother Elias Eliasson (born 1819) also came to Soda Springs with the Morrisites in 1863; Shupe lists “Elias Eliason” and “Mrs. Elias Eliason” beside Erik and Karin (p. 13). Neither is on the roll of membership. Elias’s wife was Margreta Nilsdotter (1816–1900), and the family was in the Deer Lodge Valley by 1870, some years before Erik. The Family Tree records for Elias are tangled: one (LVXJ-L2R) has his Swedish baptism, and another, which carries his wife and children, has been given Erik’s birth and death dates. An Eliason household in 1889 When Joseph Smith III, president of the RLDS Church, visited Soda Springs in 1889, he stayed in the house of an Eliason family whose head was a widow, then away at Blackfoot (Joseph Smith III and the Restoration, 1952, p. 437). Erik was still living in 1893, and Elias’s widow lived in Montana, though one of Elias’s daughters later died at Blackfoot. Who that widow was is an open question. Open questions Where were Erik and Karin between the siege of June 1862 and the move to Soda Springs in May 1863? Who was the Eliason widow at Soda Springs in 1889? In what year did Erik move to the Deer Lodge Valley, and did Karin ever join him there? The 1880 census finds him farming there alone, with the family still at Soda Springs. His homestead case file at the National Archives (Helena land office, Homestead Certificate 560) should give the date he entered the land. If you can answer one, write to contact@morrisite.org. On the roll John Parson (1829–1892) President of the Morrisite apostles, who gave the order to raise the white flag at Kington Fort in 1862, later a Morrisite leader in Nevada, and joined the RLDS Church. On the roll Parson, John, in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886 Born January 1829, England (Family Tree) Died 1892, Montana (Family Tree) June 1862 Taken at Kington Fort: printed as “John Parsons” in the Deseret News list of June 25, 1862, held to $1,500 bail for the March 1863 term Later path Stayed Morrisite, later joined the RLDS Church. Kington Fort, 1862 In the spring of 1862 Lars Gurtsen, also called Lewis C. Gurtsen, left the Morrisite camp. A party under Peter Klemgaard captured him with William Jones and John Jensen, and the three were held in a log house at the fort. After several days he and Jensen cut a hole through the log wall; Gurtsen got away, and Jensen was caught and brought back (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 98–100, 105). The Church History Department’s profile of Lars Christian Geertsen adds that he went to Salt Lake City and told the authorities that Jones and Jensen were being held against their will, and that the posse followed: the detention of these men is what brought the writs and the siege of June 1862. Salmon, Idaho The spellings of his name trace his road north. A Montana county marriage record calls him L. C. Gurtson, and the 1880 census lists him as Louis C., the “Lewis C.” of Anderson’s account; in Salmon he was known as Lars. He and his Danish wife came to the Salmon area in 1866 or 1867, as the town grew up around the gold strikes of 1866. In 1868 he homesteaded a 160-acre ranch, raising cattle to supply the miners, and a small community called Geertson Creek grew up nearby. He served for a time as a territorial justice of the peace, and he was one of the original shareholders of the Salmon City Cemetery Association. Between 1872 and 1883 he built a two-story house of hewn logs, square-notched and chinked. It also held the ranch commissary, which served settlers and travelers on the Red Rock–Salmon City stage line, and its upstairs dance hall was a gathering place for the community into the 1920s. The house was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on April 3, 1980, as the Lars Geertson House (later the Herb Aldous House). A Salmon resident reports that it was damaged by fire years ago and torn down in 2025. Lars Christian Geertsen died at Salmon in 1925 and is buried in the Salmon Cemetery. Sources Anderson, C. LeRoy. The 1880 U.S. census, taken that June, lists him at Walla Walla as “William W. Davis”, 47, a mason and a widower, with eight children from Grace, 25, to Seth, 4; Arthur and David are not among them. The census mortality schedule for the year records the deaths of Arthur Davis, 12, and David Davis, 10, of diphtheria in February 1880, and, in May, of “Sarah E. Davis”, 43, born in Wales. She was evidently his wife Anne Elizabeth: Family Tree records her birth on March 29, 1836, and her death at Walla Walla on May 19, 1879, which fits her age but falls just before the census year that began June 1, 1879 (1880 U.S. census, Walla Walla, ED 50, p. 263c, and mortality schedule, ED 50, p. 3; FamilySearch LRMD-NG6). His neighbors on that census page include Swin O. Hagg, David Park, Rachel Jones, two McCue boys and Cornelia S. Perkins, 30, who became his second wife (Find a Grave memorial 15969383). Watson prints his writings and the record of his community (Watson, pp. 111ff.). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (two files, 16 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 35854). In 1881 Davies testified that he had come to Walla Walla from Montana in the fall of 1867 with his family and the James, David Thomas and Sorenson families; Swen O. Hagg put the first party at five families, about forty people. Davies also said that “the association commenced in 1866 in Montana” and that “the doctrine of reincarnation is taught and believed”; a list he put in evidence names forty-three members in March 1881 (Watson, pp. 111ff.; Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81). The community dated its era from January 24, 1866. On May 25, 1881, the court gave Cilley, Courtney and Evans judgment against Davies for $3,225; the sheriff sold his livestock and equipment on June 11, and on July 16 the community’s eighty acres, the west half of the northwest quarter of section 34, township 7 north, range 37 east (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81). In 1885 the First National Bank of Walla Walla won a default judgment against him and his son over nine notes of 1879, made out to Lewis H. Bowman (First National Bank v. Davies, 1885). The 1870 census in the Deer Lodge Valley lists a different household: Ellen C., aged 49, and two children, Chris, 11, and Anna, 8. Ellen may be a second wife, or the enumerator may have taken the names down wrongly. Neither Ellen nor Chris appears in Family Tree, and where Maria was in 1870 is not known. By 1880 Niels was living alone. The later Becks of the valley In 1884 an eighteen-year-old Dane, Soren R. Beck, born July 9, 1866, the son of Anders and Annie (Sorenson) Beck, came alone to Deer Lodge and for three years worked on “a ranch belonging to Nels R. Beck, adjoining the city of Deer Lodge.” In 1889 he leased land on the Little Blackfoot and went on to raise horses, cattle and sheep (Progressive Men of the State of Montana, 1902, p. 1637). The biography does not say how the two were related; if Soren’s father was an Anders Rasmussen Beck, Soren may have been Niels’s nephew, but that is not yet shown. Soren’s descendants still ranch in the Deer Lodge and Avon valleys. A third Beck family, Nels Jensen Beck and Maria Helena (Hansen) Beck, who came from Denmark in 1872, is distinct from both. Open questions When did Niels reach the Deer Lodge Valley? A preemption claimant had to prove the date he settled on the land, so his case file at the National Archives (Helena land office, cash certificate 230) should give it, and with it perhaps the date the Morrisite families arrived. How was Soren R. Beck, who worked on Niels’s ranch from 1884, related to him? Where were the Becks between the court term of March 1863 and 1870? Did they go to Soda Springs with the other Morrisites? Who were Ellen C., Chris and Anna Beck of the 1870 census, and did Maria come to Montana? By 1880 Niels lived alone. Places Kington Fort South Weber, Utah. The fort at South Weber where Morris gathered his followers in 1861–62, and the siege of June 1862. MO-IMG-001 · Monument, December 2008 Built in 1853 and abandoned in 1858, then reoccupied by the Morrisites. Nothing of the fort survives; a monument to the Kington Fort–Morrisite War site, Sons of Utah Pioneers marker no. 128, was erected in August 2006 at 6600 South and 475 East (N 41.14677, W 111.96884), sponsored by the South Weber chapter of the Daughters of Utah Pioneers, the Ogden Pioneer chapter of the Sons of Utah Pioneers and All Build Construction and Landscaping, with the site designed by Douglas B. Stephens (Barlow, 2022). The fort was named for Bishop Thomas Kington, and “Kington” is the correct spelling. The monument itself notes that the earliest sources (the notebook kept by Kington’s wife, his gravestone, Wilford Woodruff’s journals, and early church records) all spell it that way; recent scholarship such as Holley (2008) follows them. Many nineteenth- and twentieth-century accounts, and some modern references, including the Utah History Encyclopedia and Wikipedia, write “Kingston Fort.” Insiders used both: Forscutt, who lived in the fort, wrote “Kingston’s Fort” and called it “the proper name” of the place (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702). Search under both spellings. A log cabin nearby, which the local historian Ed Cooper, from oral accounts of older South Weber residents, identified as the building Morris used to hold the three departing members whose detention led to the siege, is shown in MO-IMG-046–049; it has been moved from its original site, and the identification rests on local tradition. About 200 yards south, on the west side of the road, in the South Weber Pioneer Cemetery, a marker reads “Joseph Werner, ‘Morrisite,’ about 1870” (MO-IMG-021). The name lingered locally. In the early 2000s, while the editor was going door to door in South Weber, a woman then in her sixties said that elementary-school classmates had called her “Morrisite” as a taunt because of where in South Weber she lived; she said her family had no Morrisite connection. (Editor’s memorandum of recollection, written November 1, 2026; the conversation was not recorded at the time.) A cannonball from the siege was kept by the family of Al Peek, together with a portrait of Mary Christoffersen Anderson (MO-IMG-051–053; the portrait is MO-IMG-062). VisitThe monument is public. The Pioneer Cemetery appears to lie on private land but is reached by a public easement; stay on the access route. The cabin is on private property. Places on the ground The fort and the siege of June 13–15, 1862, as the sources place them. Nothing of the fort survives, and the ground is now streets, houses and fields. Solid markers are located; outlined markers are approximate (placed from a plan or a written description); the dashed square is the fort as G. Q. Jones drew it. Most of this is private land: the monument is the public place to visit. If you know where one of these places stood, please write. Streets are drawn straight through the monument corner and are approximate. The fort’s outline follows the plan by G. Q. Jones (1996) and the editor’s 2009 overlay of it on an aerial photograph; it is good to perhaps a hundred feet. The Kington Fort–Morrisite War Site monument Located 2006 map Sons of Utah Pioneers marker no. 128, at 6600 South and 475 East, erected in August 2006 by the South Weber chapter of the Daughters of Utah Pioneers, the Ogden Pioneer chapter of the Sons of Utah Pioneers and All Build Construction and Landscaping. It stands within the area of the old fort. Public. Sources: Barlow (2022); see History. Kington Fort Approximate 1853–1862 Built in 1853 by the settlers under Bishop Thomas Kington and abandoned in 1858; a square of about 645 feet with log and later adobe houses along an earth wall, gates on each side and a public square in the middle. The Morrisites reoccupied it in 1861, rebuilt the wall in adobe and built new houses. Jones’s plan places Morris’s tent and an adobe schoolhouse in the southwest part of the fort, and the intersection of today’s 6600 South and 475 East inside it. Sources: G. Q. Jones, “Morrisite Fort – Plan, South Weber, Davis County, Utah,” December 1996 (not reproduced here); the monument text. The bowery, west of the fort Approximate June 13, 1862 map The open-air meeting place in a grove of trees west of the fort. On the morning of June 13, as Morris spoke to his people there, the posse’s cannon fire fell among them, killing two women and wounding Mary Christoffersen. The marker follows Jones’s plan. Sources: Jones plan (1996); see History. The west gate and the surrender Approximate June 15, 1862 map Jones places near the west gate the scene on June 15, after the white flag was raised, in which Joseph Morris and two women were killed and John Banks was fatally wounded. Accounts of how it happened differ; see History and Questions. Sources: Jones plan (1996). The south gate and the slough Approximate June 15, 1862 map Jones’s plan marks a slough just outside the south gate, where a road crossed it, and notes that on June 15 an armored battery made from the rear of a wagon was rolled toward the fort, caught a wheel in the mud and tipped over, and that its crew retreated under musket fire. Jones gives no source for this. Anderson describes a rolling battery of willows and wagon wheels pushed up to the fort wall the same day, so the accounts differ. See MO-IMG-032 under Images. Sources: Jones plan (1996); Anderson, Revisited, p. 135. The posse on the south bluffs Approximate June 13–15, 1862 map The fort stood in a bowl on the Weber River flood plain, ringed on the south and west by sandy bluffs about half a mile off and some two hundred feet high. Burton’s posse took its position on the south bluffs on June 13 with its cannon, from which it could see into the fort. The marker stands for the bluff line, not a known gun position.

Places Morristown Soda Springs, Idaho. The settlement at Soda Springs founded in May 1863 under the protection of Patrick Edward Connor. MO-IMG-061 · Anderson gravestone, October 2018 The Morrisites were among the founders of Soda Springs, one of the oldest towns in Idaho. Connor reported bringing 160 settlers (53 families, seven single men, and four widows), who arrived May 20, 1863, and were given building lots on a town site surveyed on the north bank of the Bear River, beside the military reservation of Camp Connor (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, OR). A later marker describes a 200-acre survey west of Soda Creek, lots of 25 by 130 feet, and one-room log homes with dirt floors. The Morrisite “Lower Town” stood below the military “Upper Town”; Soda Springs was the first seat of Oneida County, 1864–66. After the troops left in 1865, hard winters and failed crops thinned the settlement. Many Morrisites moved on, some north to the Blackfoot area, and others sold to miners and to Latter-day Saint settlers, whose new town site dates from Brigham Young’s visit of 1870–71. Most of the old town now lies under Alexander Reservoir. Those who stayed, led by Niels Anderson, carried their quarrel with the Mormon hierarchy into territorial politics; the Niels Anderson Homestead marker credits his anti-polygamy campaign with helping deny Mormons the vote in Idaho. Accounts differ on some details: most give 160 settlers (one popular account says about 325), Camp Connor’s founding is dated May 20 or May 23, and the National Park Service marker wrongly calls Morris Welsh-born. Markers stand in town, including the Park Service’s Morrisite settlement marker in the parking lot of a Latter-day Saint meetinghouse (HMDB), the state’s Camp Connor marker (HMDB), and “Law & Order on the Frontier” on Camp Connor’s probable site near the hospital (HMDB). Descendants held a reunion in Soda Springs on August 3, 2013. Niels and Mary Christoffersen Anderson, married at Morristown on July 20, 1863 (the date on their gravestone; some accounts give July 30), are buried in Fairview Cemetery at Soda Springs. Their gravestone carries a long bronze inscription giving a Morrisite account of the 1862 siege, in which Mary, then fourteen, lost her jaw to the first cannon shot fired into the fort. Forscutt, who was present, described her lower jaw “hanging only by a narrow strip of skin,” with two women dead beside her (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702; MO-IMG-061, with transcription; MO-IMG-062; HMDB; see also the Niels Anderson Homestead marker). VisitThe markers and the Anderson gravestone in Fairview Cemetery are publicly accessible. The townsite is largely under Alexander Reservoir. In the chronology May 1863Many Morrisites leave Utah under the protection of Patrick Edward Connor, commanding the District of Utah. On May 5 a party of 160 (53 families, seven single men, and four widows) sets out with a company of California Volunteers; it reaches Soda Springs on May 20, where Connor has a town site surveyed on the north bank of the Bear River beside a new military post, Camp Connor (established by order of May 23). The Morrisites call their town Morristown. Connor also gives 150 Morrisites passage to Carson City, Nevada, in an empty supply train. Others settle in California. (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, Official Records, ser. 1, vol. 50, pt. 1, 226–29.) 1860s–Some Morrisites return to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, in Utah and elsewhere. The 2006 monument at South Weber notes that a few were rebaptized and remained there. Others find a home in the Reorganized Church (RLDS): the former Morrisite apostle Mark Hill Forscutt joins it in Salt Lake City in 1865, and John L. Bear (Johann Lebrecht Bär, 1838–1919), a Swiss convert from Affoltern am Albis who emigrated from Zürich in 1860 and lost his wife and child at Kington Fort, later serves as an RLDS missionary to Switzerland and Germany, dies in Independence, Missouri, and publishes his autobiography in the RLDS Journal of History. In 1865 RLDS missionaries at Malad, Idaho, baptize several people who appear on the roll. Others join only after years in the Morrisite groups: Erick and Caroline Eliason are baptized together at Soda Springs on June 9, 1870; Margaretta Cook leaves the Morrisites in Nevada in 1870 and is baptized RLDS in 1873; and Lena Hanson, at Soda Springs and then Deer Lodge, in 1895 (see the roll).
