Danish-speaking congregations whose 1869 membership and account books survive in translation. VisitNo sites identified; the record survives in documents only. In the chronology 1869Danish-language congregations keep membership and account books in Omaha, Nebraska, and Council Bluffs, Iowa. 1870sMany members regather in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, under George Williams, the “Prophet Cainan,” who claims to be Morris's successor. In 1874 the Montana church is divided into two stakes. A local history of Anaconda dates the first Morrisite settlers in the valley to 1863, among them William Price Thomas on Warm Springs Creek, east of the later townsite; has a group under William James arriving in 1867 as others left; and describes a caravan of thirteen covered wagons that came in June 1871, part of a larger migration from Iowa, Nebraska, Utah and Idaho: Scandinavian families, mostly Danes, with English, Scottish and Welsh believers. It places the two congregations in the upper valley near Lost Creek and near Race Track Creek, with about eighty members in all (Patrick F. Morris, Anaconda, Montana, 1997, pp. 15–17). s: Places Deer Lodge Valley Powell and Deer Lodge counties, Montana. The longest-lived center of the movement, and the Lord’s House at Racetrack, the last Morrisite church standing. MO-IMG-014 · Racetrack church, November 2018 The longest-lived center of the movement. The wood-frame Morrisite church, begun in 1877, still stands on private land at Racetrack, about 8 miles south of Deer Lodge: on the north side of Dempsey Road, just west of the railroad and the Interstate 90 frontage road (Exit 195; about 46.29° N, 112.75° W; NE¼ sec. 8, T6N R9W, Powell County). The county lists it as a frame building of 18 by 36 feet (Montana Cadastral, Montana State Library, consulted November 6, 2026). It was last photographed for this guide in November 2018. Called the Lord’s House, as the panel over its doors reads, it was the church’s meeting place: George Thompson was elected president of the church there in 1886, and Andrew Hendrikson (1886–1921) and George Johnson (1921–1954) presided over the Montana church from it. It is the only Morrisite church building known to survive, and its condition has worsened markedly since 2009. See the condition record under Images. View onlyThe church is privately owned, unsafe and not open to the public. View it from Dempsey Road or the frontage road; do not enter the property. Solid markers are located; outlined markers are approximate; squares are land patents, drawn at the quarter-section or section the patent names. Sites not yet located are listed without a marker. If you know where one of these places stood, please write. “Willow Glen Ranch” near Opportunity, shown in grey, is the later company stock farm of that name (burned in 1963), not the Willow Glen of 1881. The Lord’s House, Racetrack Located 1877–1969 map The church of the Montana Morrisites, begun in 1877, on the north side of Dempsey Road just west of the railroad and the Interstate 90 frontage road (NE¼ sec. 8, T6N R9W, Powell County). George Thompson was elected president of the church here on May 10, 1886. It is the only Morrisite church building known to survive. Privately owned and unsafe: view it from the road only. Sources: Montana Cadastral, Montana State Library, consulted November 6, 2026; Anderson, Revisited. See the photographs under Images. The earliest is Niels R. Beck’s preemption entry, patented in 1871. On the map each patent is a square at the quarter-section or section it names: that locates the land, not the house. Willow Glen: the post office and the old log church Approximate 1881 (the church earlier) map In August 1881 a California family named Eardley built a log store at a crossroads where the road to Philipsburg left the Butte stage road, named it Willow Glen, and had it made a post office. Eliza Eardley Hardin, then eight, remembered “an old log church and a large fenced yard” near the crossroads, and next to it the home of William James, the Morrisites’ local president. The church was very probably the Willow Glen Meeting House on Warm Springs Creek where the church court met on May 10, 1882, and sustained James as president. The marker is the federal gazetteer’s point for the Willow Glen post office, between Anaconda and Warm Springs; the church has not been located exactly. Sources: Eliza Eardley Hardin, reminiscence, SC 788, Montana Historical Society Research Center, Helena; U.S. Geographic Names Information System, “Willowglen Post Office (historical)”; Anderson, Revisited. William Price Thomas on Warm Springs Creek Approximate 1863 map A local history names William Price Thomas, a Welshman and confidant of George Williams, among the first Morrisites in the valley, settling in 1863 on Warm Springs Creek about three miles east of where Anaconda would be built. His sons John, Evan, Frank and Daniel later homesteaded nearby. The marker follows that description only. Sources: Patrick F. Morris, Anaconda, Montana (1997), p. 15. The upper-valley congregation “near Lost Creek” Not yet located 1870s–1880s The church in Montana was organized as two stakes in 1874. Morris places one congregation “in the upper valley near Lost Creek” and the other near Deer Lodge by Race Track Creek, each with a meeting house and a school. Lost Creek runs east past Galen to the Clark Fork, a few miles north of Willow Glen, so the upper-valley meeting house may be the Willow Glen church; this has not been confirmed. Sources: Patrick F. Morris, Anaconda, Montana (1997), p. 16; Anderson, Revisited. Gregson Hot Springs (now Fairmont) Approximate 1860s? map An Anaconda historian, interviewed in 1989, said the first Morrisites stayed at the hot springs later named Gregson “a winter or two” before homesteading in the valley. No earlier source for this has been found. Morris says Ben

s: Places Kingdom of Heaven Walla Walla, Washington. William W. Davies’s community near Walla Walla, 1867–1881. William W. Davies's commune near Walla Walla, 1867–1881. Its site lay on the west side of Mormon Grade Road, a few hundred yards south of Scenic Loop Road, near Russell Creek (Dan Clark, Walla Walla 2020, correspondence with the editor, November 2026). An interpretive sign that Walla Walla 2020 put up at the corner of Scenic Loop and Mormon Grade roads was shot up, replaced, shot up again and finally stolen. The road name and Davies’s grave in Lyons Cemetery remain. VisitLyons Cemetery is public. The colony site is not marked. The colony’s eighty acres Located 1867–1881 map After the 1881 judgment against Davies, the sheriff levied on his land, “the W½ NW¼ sec. 34, T7N R37E,” less one acre, and sold it at the courthouse door on July 16, 1881, for $1,975. A witness in the case spoke of the eighty acres “where he resides,” so this was almost certainly the camp. The tract lies on the west side of Mormon Grade Road just south of its corner with Scenic Loop Road, which matches Dan Clark’s placing of the site near Russell Creek. Private land; the site is not marked. Sources: Wikipedia, “William W. Davies.” In the chronology 1867–1881William W. Davies leads a Morrisite offshoot, the Kingdom of Heaven, near Walla Walla, Washington. He declares his infant son Arthur to be Christ returned, the “Walla Walla Jesus.” Lawsuits by former members end the community: in 1881 a court awards three of them $3,225, and the sheriff sells the community’s livestock and its eighty acres to satisfy the judgment.
